To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the developmental decrease in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is correlated with morphological and physiological changes in pedunculo pontine nucleus neurons.

the largest decrease in rat REM sleep occurs at a time when cholinergic PPS neurons double in size, the proportion of cells with short AP duration increases and the proportion of cells having long AP durations decreases, and Ih current increases.

the largest decrease in rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep (10-30 days) is associated with a doubling in the size of pedunculopotine nucleus (PPCN) neurons, and a decrease in the number of neurons with long action potential duration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the developmental decrease in the amount of REM sleep in the infant rat and man.
the development of a brain region that plays a major role in the control of REM sleep.
understanding the mechanisms that regulate REM sleep and arousal in man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the developmental changes in cholinergic PPM neurons are associated with the decrease in REM sleep.
PPN neurons are not only morphologically but also physiologically different in the rat during the developmental decrease in sleep.
the developmental decrease in cholinergic PPM neurons and the decrease in Ih current may be involved in the developmental decrease in the amount of REM sleep.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decrease in REM sleep is associated with changes in the properties of PPN cholinergic cells that are involved in the control REM sleep and arousal.

PPN cholinergic cells undergo a period of maturation between 12 and14 days, when they are the largest and most excitable, then become smaller and less excitable by 21 days, when the largest decrease in the proportion of REM sleep occurs.

during the developmental decrease in sleep, PPN neurons undergo a period of maturation, with cholinergic cells increasing in cell area, AP duration, and AHP duration, and noncholinergics decreasing in AP duration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PPN neurons undergo a period of developmental plasticity that is correlated with a decrease in REM sleep, and that this developmental plasticity may be important for the control of REM sleep.

the developmental decrease in the proportion of cholinergic cells with long AP duration and Ih current, and the increase in the proportion of noncholinergic neurons with short AP duration and short AHP, may underlie the developmental decrease in cholinergic drive and REM sleep, respectively, during the period when the largest decrease in sleep REM occurs.
the decrease in REM sleep is paralleled by developmental changes in PPN cells.
